title: Choice and Strategy
description: Structured approaches to decisions, trade-offs, and action.

questions.prompt: When is a reversible decision often best made quickly?
options: When delay costs more than a safe trial and learning
questions.explanation: Fast, reversible experiments can create information; consequential irreversible decisions warrant greater care.

questions.prompt: A decision matrix can make criteria and trade-offs more explicit.
questions.explanation: Matrices organize comparisons but do not remove value judgments about criteria or weights.

questions.prompt: The option with the highest score on a weighted matrix is objectively best.
questions.explanation: Weights and scores encode assumptions and preferences; sensitivity checks are important.

questions.prompt: Which are useful before committing to a major decision?
questions.explanation: Clear objectives and constraints make alternatives comparable and avoid solving the wrong problem.

questions.prompt: A pre-mortem asks a team to imagine a plan failed and identify plausible causes.
questions.explanation: The exercise can surface neglected risks before commitment and encourage specific mitigations.

questions.prompt: What does opportunity cost mean?
options: The value of the best alternative forgone
The total price of a choice
A cost that cannot be estimated
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost reflects the next-best use of scarce resources.

questions.prompt: A decision rule should match the stakes and reversibility of the choice.
questions.explanation: High-consequence or hard-to-reverse choices generally merit more evidence and review.

questions.prompt: Which help distinguish a decision from an outcome?
options: Record what was known at decision time
Judge only by whether luck favored the choice
questions.explanation: A sound process can yield a bad outcome by chance; contemporaneous records help avoid outcome bias.

questions.prompt: A good decision process guarantees a good outcome.
questions.explanation: Uncertainty and chance mean even well-reasoned choices can have poor outcomes.

questions.prompt: A robust decision is one that:
questions.explanation: Robustness favors acceptable performance across scenarios rather than optimality under one fragile forecast.

questions.prompt: Which can improve a group decision?
questions.explanation: Independent views and explicit assumption checks reduce conformity and reveal information gaps.

questions.prompt: A stopping rule can limit repeated searching when new information is unlikely to change the choice.
questions.explanation: Predefined stopping criteria can reduce delay and prevent endless search for certainty.

questions.prompt: More information always improves a decision enough to justify its cost.
questions.explanation: Information has acquisition and delay costs; its value depends on whether it could change action.

questions.prompt: What is a decision threshold?
options: A value at which the preferred action changes
A final answer with no uncertainty
questions.explanation: Thresholds connect evidence to action, such as when expected benefit outweighs cost or risk.

questions.prompt: Which are elements of a useful implementation plan?
questions.explanation: Ownership, milestones, metrics, and triggers connect a choice to adaptation and execution.

questions.prompt: Defaults can influence choices even when alternatives remain available.
questions.explanation: Defaults change effort and perceived recommendation, so their rationale and opt-out path matter.

questions.prompt: A decision with a high expected value must be chosen regardless of distribution or fairness.
questions.explanation: Expected value is one input; constraints, downside risk, rights, and distribution may also govern.

questions.prompt: When values conflict, a useful first step is to:
options: Name the values and trade-offs explicitly
Hide the trade-off in a score
Assume all stakeholders value the same things
questions.explanation: Explicit values help clarify disagreement and make compromises reviewable.

questions.prompt: Which support learning from a decision?
options: Change success criteria after seeing results
questions.explanation: Predefined metrics and review points reduce hindsight and enable a fair evaluation.

questions.prompt: A small pilot can be valuable when it is safe, informative, and connected to a decision.
questions.explanation: A pilot is useful when it tests a meaningful uncertainty and its results can change the next step.
